statute_title: Driving Under the Influence of Alcohol
offense_class: Misdemeanor (first through third); Felony (fourth+ or with injury)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence of an alcoholic beverage
Defendant's ability to drive safely was impaired by alcohol
enhancements: Minor under 14 in vehicle (child endangerment under Cal. Penal Code § 273a)
Fourth or subsequent DUI (felony under Cal. Veh. Code § 23550)
notes: California implied consent law under Cal. Veh. Code § 23612. Separate DMV administrative license suspension. DUI school required: 3-month (first), 18-month (second), 30-month (third). IID required for repeat offenses statewide.

statute_title: Driving with BAC .08% or Higher — First Offense
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle
At the time of driving, defendant's blood alcohol concentration was .08% or more
mandatory_minimum: 96 hours (if probation granted); no mandatory jail if probation with conditions
enhancements: Refusal of chemical test (additional license suspension)
notes: Probation typically 3-5 years. 3-month DUI school required. License suspension 4-6 months. IID available as alternative to full suspension.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle
While under the influence of alcohol or with BAC .08% or higher
One or more prior DUI convictions within 10 years
enhancements: Third DUI within 10 years (Cal. Veh. Code § 23546)
Fourth or subsequent DUI (felony under Cal. Veh. Code § 23550)
notes: 18-month or 30-month DUI school required. 2-year license suspension (second); 3-year revocation (third). IID mandatory. Fourth DUI is a wobbler (felony or misdemeanor).

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence of Drugs
offense_class: Misdemeanor (first through third); Felony (fourth+ or with injury)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence of a drug
Drug impaired defendant's ability to drive with the caution of a sober person
mandatory_minimum: Same escalation as alcohol DUI for repeat offenses
enhancements: Combined alcohol and drug use (Cal. Veh. Code § 23152(g))
Causing injury while DUI drugs (Cal. Veh. Code § 23153)
notes: No per se drug limit in California. Prosecution must prove impairment. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluation commonly used. Includes prescription drugs, marijuana, and controlled substances.

elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Defendant knew of its presence
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
Substance was a usable amount
enhancements: Prior sex offense or violent felony conviction (may be charged as felony)
Possession near a school (Cal. Health & Safety Code § 11353.5)
notes: Prop 47 (2014) reduced most simple possession from felony to misdemeanor. Eligible for drug diversion under Cal. Penal Code § 1000 or Prop 36. Covers Schedule I-IV substances including heroin, cocaine, and certain prescription drugs.

elements: Defendant possessed cannabis
Amount exceeded legal limit for personal use (28.5g flower or 8g concentrate)
Defendant was not authorized under state law
notes: Prop 64 (2016) legalized recreational cannabis for adults 21+. Up to 28.5g flower or 8g concentrate is legal. Possession with intent to sell remains illegal under § 11359.

elements: Defendant possessed methamphetamine or other specified substance
Defendant knew of its presence
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
Substance was a usable amount
enhancements: Prior conviction for sex offense or specified violent felony (may be charged as felony)
notes: Reduced to misdemeanor by Prop 47 for simple possession. Covers methamphetamine, PCP, GHB, and certain other stimulants/hallucinogens. Drug diversion available.

elements: Defendant possessed cocaine
Defendant knew of its presence
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
Substance was a usable amount
enhancements: Prior sex offense or violent felony conviction (may be charged as felony)
notes: Cocaine is a Schedule II substance. Prosecuted under § 11350(a). Possession for sale under § 11351 is a felony (2-4 years).

elements: Defendant possessed an opiate or opioid controlled substance
Defendant knew of its presence
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
Substance was a usable amount
enhancements: Prior sex offense or violent felony conviction (may be charged as felony)
notes: Includes heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, and other opioids. Prop 47 reduced to misdemeanor. Drug diversion available under Cal. Penal Code § 1000.

statute_title: Possession of Controlled Prescription Drug Without Prescription
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled prescription drug
Defendant did not have a valid prescription
Defendant knew of its presence and nature
notes: Covers Schedule II-IV prescription drugs possessed without a valid prescription. Doctor-shopping prosecuted under Cal. Health & Safety Code § 11173.

statute_title: Possession of Controlled Substance for Sale
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Defendant knew of its presence and nature
Substance was in a usable amount
Defendant possessed the substance with the intent to sell it
enhancements: Large quantity (3-25 years additional under Cal. Health & Safety Code § 11370.4)
Prior drug sale conviction (3 years additional per prior)
notes: Not eligible for Prop 47 reduction. Intent to sell inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, pay-owe sheets, large cash. Covers heroin, cocaine, and other Schedule I-II narcotics.

statute_title: Transportation or Sale of a Controlled Substance
penalty_max: 5 years (3-5 triad); 9 years if transported across 2+ county lines
elements: Defendant sold, transported, furnished, or gave away a controlled substance
Defendant knew of the substance's presence
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
enhancements: Transportation across two or more county lines (3-9 year triad)
notes: Covers sale, transport, administration, furnishing, or giving away of Schedule I-II narcotics. Transportation means movement for purposes of sale, not merely carrying for personal use.

elements: Defendant manufactured, compounded, converted, produced, derived, processed, or prepared a controlled substance
Defendant knew of the substance's nature as a controlled substance
enhancements: Causing great bodily injury or death
notes: Commonly charged for methamphetamine labs. Also covers extraction or chemical synthesis of controlled substances. Offering to manufacture is also charged under § 11379.6(a).

elements: Defendant committed an underlying drug offense (§ 11351, § 11352, etc.)
The substance involved exceeded specified weight thresholds
Defendant knew of the substance and its quantity
mandatory_minimum: 3 years additional (1+ kg cocaine/heroin); 5 years (4+ kg); 10 years (10+ kg); 15 years (20+ kg); 20 years (40+ kg); 25 years (80+ kg)
notes: Weight enhancement statute — adds consecutive prison time to underlying drug offense. Applies to cocaine, cocaine base, heroin, and methamphetamine. Amounts measured in aggregate weight.

elements: Defendant possessed a device, contrivance, instrument, or paraphernalia
Used for unlawfully injecting or smoking a controlled substance specified in § 11054-11058
notes: Covers pipes, syringes (when used for illegal drugs), and other smoking/injection devices. Authorized needle exchange participants are exempt.

elements: Defendant did an act that by its nature would directly and probably result in the application of force to a person
Defendant did that act willfully
Defendant was aware of facts that would lead a reasonable person to realize the act would directly and probably result in application of force
Defendant had the present ability to apply force
enhancements: Against a peace officer or firefighter (Cal. Penal Code § 241(c))
notes: Assault is the attempt to commit a battery — no contact required. Simple assault is always a misdemeanor in California.

elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully used force or violence upon another person
enhancements: Serious bodily injury (Cal. Penal Code § 243(d) — wobbler, up to 4 years)
Against a peace officer (Cal. Penal Code § 243(b)-(c))
notes: Battery requires actual physical contact (even slight touching). Simple battery is misdemeanor. Battery with serious bodily injury is a wobbler.

statute_title: Assault by Means of Force Likely to Produce Great Bodily Injury
elements: Defendant did an act that by its nature would directly and probably result in the application of force to a person
Force used was likely to produce great bodily injury
Defendant did the act willfully
Defendant was aware the act would produce such a result
Defendant had the present ability to apply such force
enhancements: Great bodily injury actually caused (additional 3-6 years under Cal. Penal Code § 12022.7)
Against a peace officer or firefighter
notes: Wobbler offense — may be charged as felony or misdemeanor based on severity of force and circumstances. 'Great bodily injury' means significant or substantial injury beyond what is inherent in the offense.

elements: Defendant did an act that by its nature would directly and probably result in the application of force to a person
Defendant did that act with a deadly weapon or instrument other than a firearm
Defendant acted willfully
Defendant had the present ability to apply force with the weapon
enhancements: Use of a firearm (Cal. Penal Code § 245(a)(2) — 2-4 years; § 245(d) up to 12 years if semiautomatic against peace officer)
Great bodily injury inflicted (additional 3-6 years under § 12022.7)
notes: A 'deadly weapon' is any object, instrument, or weapon used in a manner capable of causing death or great bodily injury. Strike offense under California Three Strikes law.

elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully used force or violence upon another person
The force used caused serious bodily injury
notes: Serious bodily injury means a serious impairment of physical condition including but not limited to loss of consciousness, concussion, bone fracture, protracted loss of any bodily member or organ, wound requiring extensive suturing, or serious disfigurement.

statute_title: Corporal Injury to Spouse or Cohabitant
elements: Defendant willfully inflicted corporal injury on a spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, former cohabitant, or parent of defendant's child
The injury resulted in a traumatic condition
enhancements: Prior DV conviction within 7 years (felony, 2-5 year triad under § 273.5(f))
notes: Traumatic condition means a wound or bodily injury caused by physical force. Mandatory 52-week batterer's treatment program. Protective order issued. Firearm prohibition under Cal. Penal Code § 29825.

elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully touched a spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, former cohabitant, fiancé/fiancée, or dating partner
The touching was harmful or offensive
notes: No visible injury required (unlike § 273.5). Mandatory 52-week batterer's treatment program. Commonly charged as alternative or lesser-included offense to § 273.5.

elements: Defendant willfully threatened to commit a crime that would result in death or great bodily injury to another person
Defendant made the threat with the specific intent that it be taken as a threat
The threat was so clear, immediate, unconditional, and specific as to convey a gravity of purpose and immediate prospect of execution
The threat caused the other person to be in sustained fear for their safety or their immediate family's safety
The fear was reasonable
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon in making threat (additional 1 year)
notes: Strike offense under Three Strikes law when charged as felony. Threat can be verbal, written, or electronic. 'Sustained fear' means fear for a period of time beyond momentary, fleeting, or transitory.

elements: Defendant committed an unlawful killing of a human being or fetus
With malice aforethought
The killing was willful, deliberate, and premeditated, OR committed during the perpetration of specified felonies (felony murder)
enhancements: Special circumstances (Cal. Penal Code § 190.2 — LWOP or death)
notes: First degree includes premeditated murder, felony murder (during robbery, burglary, arson, rape, carjacking, etc.), murder by poison, lying in wait, or destructive device. Strike offense.

elements: Defendant committed an unlawful killing of a human being or fetus
With malice aforethought
The killing was not willful, deliberate, and premeditated (implied malice)
enhancements: Prior murder conviction (25 years to life)
Victim was a peace officer (25 years to life)
notes: Second degree murder covers killings with implied malice — defendant acted with conscious disregard for human life. Includes DUI Watson murder (prior knowledge of danger). Strike offense.

penalty_max: Life with possibility of parole (premeditated); 9 years (not premeditated: 5-7-9 triad)
elements: Defendant took a direct but ineffective step toward killing another person
Defendant intended to kill that person
notes: Specific intent to kill required — intent to injure is insufficient. Strike offense. Premeditated attempted murder carries life with possibility of parole.

elements: Defendant killed another person without lawful justification
The killing was committed in a sudden quarrel or heat of passion, OR upon an honest but unreasonable belief in the need for self-defense
notes: Often a lesser included offense of murder. Heat of passion requires legally adequate provocation that would cause a reasonable person to act rashly. Strike offense.

elements: Defendant committed a crime or lawful act in an unlawful manner
The act was dangerous to human life under the circumstances
Defendant acted with criminal negligence
Defendant's act caused the death of another person
notes: Criminal negligence means more than ordinary negligence — defendant's act shows a disregard for human life or indifference to consequences. Not a strike offense.

penalty_max: 6 years (felony with gross negligence: 2-4-6 triad); 1 year (misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle
While committing an unlawful act (not a felony) or lawful act in an unlawful manner
The act was committed with gross negligence (felony) or ordinary negligence (misdemeanor)
The act caused the death of another person
enhancements: While intoxicated (Cal. Penal Code § 191.5 — up to 10 years)
notes: Gross negligence vehicular manslaughter is a wobbler. Vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated under § 191.5 is a separate, more serious offense.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle while intoxicated
While driving, committed an additional unlawful act or lawful act in an unlawful manner
The act was committed with gross negligence
The act caused the death of another person
enhancements: Prior DUI conviction (15 years to life under Cal. Penal Code § 191.5(d))
notes: Gross negligence means more than ordinary carelessness. With a prior DUI, penalty increases to 15 years to life. Second-degree Watson murder may be charged instead if defendant had prior DUI knowledge. Strike offense.

penalty_max: 9 years (first degree: 3-6-9 triad); 5 years (second degree: 2-3-5 triad)
elements: Defendant took personal property in the possession of another
From the other person or their immediate presence
Against that person's will
By means of force or fear
With the intent to permanently deprive the person of the property
notes: First degree: robbery of inhabited dwelling, driver/passenger of transit, or person at ATM. All other robberies are second degree. Strike offense under Three Strikes law.

elements: All elements of robbery under § 211
Defendant personally used a firearm during the commission of the robbery
mandatory_minimum: 10 years additional (personal use); 20 years additional (discharge); 25-to-life (discharge causing GBI/death)
enhancements: 25-to-life (discharge causing great bodily injury or death)
notes: Firearm enhancements under § 12022.53 are mandatory and consecutive to the base term. Serious and violent felony — two strikes under Three Strikes law.

penalty_max: 6 years (first degree: 2-4-6 triad); 3 years (second degree felony: 16mo-2-3 triad); 1 year (second degree misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant entered a building, room, or locked vehicle
With the intent to commit theft or any felony
notes: First degree is residential burglary (always a felony and a strike). Second degree is commercial burglary (wobbler). Entry may be by any part of the body or instrument. Intent must exist at time of entry.

elements: Defendant entered an inhabited dwelling house or other inhabited building
With the intent to commit theft or any felony
notes: Always a felony and always a strike under Three Strikes. 'Inhabited' means currently being used for dwelling purposes, whether or not someone is home. Not eligible for Prop 47 reduction.

elements: Defendant entered a commercial building or non-inhabited structure
With the intent to commit theft or any felony
notes: Wobbler — charged as felony or misdemeanor depending on facts. Shoplifting of $950 or less from open business is petty theft under Prop 47, not burglary.

elements: Defendant took personal property owned by someone else
Without the owner's consent
With the intent to permanently deprive the owner of the property
Defendant moved the property and kept it for some period of time
Property value was $950 or less
enhancements: Three or more prior theft convictions (eligible for felony under Cal. Penal Code § 666)
notes: Petty theft applies to property valued at $950 or less (raised from $400 by Prop 47). Includes theft by larceny, trick, embezzlement, and false pretenses.

elements: Defendant took personal property owned by someone else
Without the owner's consent
With the intent to permanently deprive the owner of the property
Property value exceeded $950, OR property was a firearm, automobile, or taken from the person
notes: Grand theft of a firearm is always a felony. Grand theft auto covered under § 487(d)(1). Grand theft from the person under § 487(c) is always a felony.

elements: Defendant entered a commercial establishment during regular business hours
With the intent to commit larceny
Value of property taken or intended to be taken was $950 or less
enhancements: Prior serious felony conviction may allow felony prosecution
notes: Created by Prop 47. Shoplifting of $950 or less is always a misdemeanor regardless of prior criminal history (with narrow exceptions). Cannot be charged as burglary.

elements: Defendant took personal property of another
Without the owner's consent
With intent to permanently deprive the owner
Property value was $950 or less
enhancements: Prior theft convictions (felony petty theft under § 666 with qualifying priors)
notes: Same as theft-larceny for $950 or less. Diversion programs available for first offenders in many counties.

statute_title: Unlawful Taking or Driving of a Vehicle
elements: Defendant drove or took a vehicle belonging to another person
Without the owner's consent
With the intent to permanently or temporarily deprive the owner of possession
enhancements: Prior vehicle theft conviction (additional 1 year under Cal. Penal Code § 666.5)
notes: Differs from grand theft auto (§ 487(d)) in that temporary taking is sufficient. Does not require intent to permanently deprive. Wobbler offense.

elements: Defendant bought, received, concealed, sold, or withheld property
The property had been stolen or obtained through extortion
Defendant knew the property was stolen or obtained through extortion
notes: Victim can sue civilly for treble damages under § 496(c). Cannot be convicted of both theft and receiving the same property. Value threshold of $950 determines felony/misdemeanor under Prop 47.

elements: Defendant willfully obtained personal identifying information belonging to another person
Defendant used that information for any unlawful purpose
Without consent of the person whose information was used
enhancements: Use in connection with a felony (additional consecutive term)
notes: Personal identifying information includes name, SSN, driver's license number, credit card number, bank account number. Each unauthorized use can be a separate count.

elements: Defendant knowingly and intentionally deceived another person with a false pretense
The deception was made with the intent to persuade the person to let the defendant take possession of their property
The person was persuaded by the false pretense to let the defendant take the property
enhancements: Victim is elderly or dependent adult (additional term)
notes: False pretense must be corroborated — the victim's testimony alone is insufficient. Corroboration can be a writing, testimony of two witnesses, or something false actually pretended.

statute_title: Fraudulent Use of an Access Card
offense_class: Wobbler (Felony if >$950 in any consecutive 6 months; Misdemeanor if ≤$950)
elements: Defendant used an access card (credit or debit card) to obtain goods, services, or money
The card was forged, expired, revoked, or obtained without consent
Defendant knew the card was invalid or not their own
notes: Multiple uses can be aggregated over a 6-month period to reach the $950 felony threshold. Separate statutes cover card theft (§ 484e), card forgery (§ 484f), and retailer fraud (§ 484h).

elements: Defendant signed another person's name, or falsely made, altered, forged, or counterfeited a document
With the intent to defraud
notes: Covers checks, money orders, contracts, deeds, bonds, and other legal documents. Forgery of a check for $950 or less is treated as a misdemeanor under Prop 47. Must be a document that could deceive a reasonable person.

elements: The owner entrusted their property to the defendant
The owner did so because they trusted the defendant
Defendant fraudulently converted or used the property for their own benefit
Defendant intended to deprive the owner of the use of the property
enhancements: Embezzlement from elder or dependent adult (additional term)
notes: Embezzlement is a form of theft where defendant had lawful possession through a relationship of trust. Includes employee theft, fiduciary misappropriation, and public officer embezzlement.

fine_max: $50,000 or double the amount of the fraud
elements: Defendant knowingly presented or caused to be presented a false or fraudulent claim for payment of a loss or injury
To an insurance company
notes: Covers auto insurance fraud, health insurance fraud, workers' comp fraud, and property insurance fraud. Separate statutes address specific types: workers' comp (§ 550), healthcare (§ 550), and automobile staging (§ 550(a)(3)).

elements: Defendant made, drew, uttered, or delivered a check
Knowing at the time there were insufficient funds to cover the check
With intent to defraud
notes: Must prove defendant knew funds were insufficient at time of writing. Total amount of bad checks can be aggregated to determine felony/misdemeanor threshold.

statute_title: Carrying a Loaded Firearm in Public
offense_class: Wobbler (Felony with priors or prohibited person; Misdemeanor otherwise)
elements: Defendant carried a loaded firearm on their person or in a vehicle
While in a public place or on a public street in an incorporated city, or on a public street or highway
mandatory_minimum: 3 months (if not a legal resident or has prior felony/firearm conviction)
enhancements: Not the registered owner of the firearm
Active participant in a criminal street gang
notes: California does not allow open carry of loaded firearms in public. Concealed carry requires a CCW permit (Cal. Penal Code § 26150). Recent changes following NYSRPA v. Bruen.

statute_title: Felon in Possession of a Firearm
elements: Defendant had been convicted of a felony
Defendant owned, purchased, received, or had in their possession a firearm
enhancements: Armed with a firearm during a felony (additional 1-5 years under § 12022)
notes: Applies to anyone convicted of any felony, certain misdemeanors (domestic violence, assault), and certain mental health holds. Lifetime prohibition for felons. Firearm includes pistols, revolvers, rifles, and shotguns.

offense_class: Wobbler (Felony or Misdemeanor depending on weapon type)
elements: Defendant possessed, manufactured, sold, or gave away a prohibited weapon
The weapon falls within the categories listed in Cal. Penal Code § 16590
notes: Prohibited weapons include switchblades, brass knuckles, shurikens, nunchaku, short-barreled shotguns/rifles, zip guns, and certain other weapons. Each weapon type has its own code section under § 16590.

statute_title: Shooting at an Inhabited Dwelling or Occupied Vehicle
elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously discharged a firearm
At an inhabited dwelling house, occupied building, occupied motor vehicle, occupied aircraft, inhabited housecar, or inhabited camper
enhancements: Great bodily injury caused (additional 3-6 years under § 12022.7)
notes: Strike offense under Three Strikes law. 'Inhabited' means currently being used for dwelling purposes. Negligent discharge under § 246.3 is a wobbler with lesser penalties.

elements: Defendant had sexual intercourse with another person
The other person did not consent to the intercourse
The act was accomplished by force, violence, duress, menace, or fear of bodily injury, OR the victim was incapable of giving consent due to intoxication, unconsciousness, or mental disability
enhancements: Multiple victims (additional 15 years to life under One Strike law § 667.61)
notes: Strike offense under Three Strikes. Mandatory sex offender registration under Cal. Penal Code § 290. Lifetime registration for most rape convictions. One Strike law (§ 667.61) applies 25-to-life for rape with specified aggravating factors.

elements: Defendant touched an intimate part of another person
The touching was against the person's will
The touching was for the specific purpose of sexual arousal, sexual gratification, or sexual abuse
enhancements: Victim was institutionalized and incapacitated (felony under § 243.4(b))
notes: Misdemeanor sexual battery under § 243.4(e)(1) covers non-aggravated cases. Felony requires victim being restrained, institutionalized, or fraudulently induced. Sex offender registration required.

penalty_max: 6 months (1 year if victim was employee, customer, or passenger)
elements: Defendant touched an intimate part of another person
Against the person's will
For the purpose of sexual arousal, sexual gratification, or sexual abuse
notes: Lesser offense than felony sexual battery. Sex offender registration may be required. Community service or counseling may be ordered.

statute_title: Unlawful Sexual Intercourse with a Minor
penalty_max: 4 years (felony if defendant 21+ and victim under 16); 1 year (misdemeanor if within 3 years of age)
elements: Defendant had sexual intercourse with a minor (under 18)
Defendant was not married to the minor
enhancements: Defendant 21+ and victim under 16 (felony under § 261.5(d), 2-3-4 triad)
notes: Misdemeanor if age difference is 3 years or less. Wobbler if age difference is more than 3 years. Felony if defendant is 21+ and victim is under 16. Civil penalties also apply.

statute_title: Child Abuse — Corporal Punishment or Injury
elements: Defendant willfully inflicted cruel or inhuman corporal punishment or injury upon a child
Resulting in a traumatic condition
enhancements: Prior child abuse conviction (additional 4 years under § 273d(b))
Great bodily injury to child under 5 (additional 4-6 years under § 12022.7(d))
notes: Traumatic condition means a wound or bodily injury caused by physical force. Does not require visible injury. Mandatory child abuse reporting triggers investigation.

elements: Defendant had care or custody of a child
Defendant willfully caused or permitted the child to be placed in a situation where the child's health was endangered
Defendant acted under circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death (felony) or not (misdemeanor)
enhancements: Great bodily injury or death results
notes: Covers a wide range of conduct: leaving children unattended in dangerous situations, allowing access to drugs, reckless driving with children in vehicle. Felony if circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death.

penalty_max: 6 years (distribution: 16mo-2-3 triad, doubled); 1 year to 3 years (possession)
elements: Defendant knowingly sent, transported, possessed, or distributed matter depicting a minor in sexual conduct
Defendant knew the matter depicted a minor engaging in sexual conduct
enhancements: Production of material (§ 311.4 — up to 8 years)
notes: Possession under § 311.11 is a wobbler. Distribution under § 311.1 is a felony. Production under § 311.4 is a felony. Sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant took, held, or detained another person by using force or fear
Defendant moved the other person a substantial distance
The other person did not consent to the movement
Defendant did not actually and reasonably believe the person consented
enhancements: For ransom or extortion (life with possibility of parole under § 209(a))
During carjacking (life with possibility of parole under § 209.5)
For sexual assault (25 years to life under § 667.61)
notes: Strike offense under Three Strikes. 'Substantial distance' means more than slight or trivial and increases risk of harm. Aggravated kidnapping (for ransom, robbery, rape) carries life sentence.

penalty_max: 9 years (structure: 2-4-6 triad; inhabited structure: 3-5-8 triad; causing GBI: 5-7-9 triad)
elements: Defendant set fire to or burned or caused the burning of a structure, forest land, or property
Defendant acted willfully and maliciously
notes: Strike offense. Arson of an inhabited structure or causing great bodily injury triggers higher triads. Reckless burning under § 452 is a wobbler with lesser penalties.

elements: Defendant maliciously defaced with graffiti or other inscribed material, damaged, or destroyed real or personal property
The property belonged to another person
enhancements: Damage to a place of worship, cemetery, or school (enhanced penalties)
notes: Felony threshold is $400 in damage. Fine can be up to $50,000 if damage is $10,000 or more, or $10,000 if damage is between $400 and $10,000. Community service and graffiti removal may be ordered.

elements: Defendant maliciously damaged or destroyed property belonging to another
Damage was less than $400
notes: California uses the term 'vandalism' rather than 'criminal mischief.' Under $400 is always a misdemeanor.

statute_title: Resisting, Obstructing, or Delaying a Peace Officer
elements: Defendant willfully resisted, delayed, or obstructed a peace officer, EMT, or firefighter
The officer was engaged in the performance of their duties
Defendant knew or reasonably should have known the person was a peace officer engaged in their duties
notes: Commonly charged alongside other offenses. Does not require physical resistance — verbal interference or fleeing can qualify. Officer must be acting lawfully at the time.

statute_title: Obstructing Justice / Obstructing a Peace Officer
elements: Defendant willfully resisted, delayed, or obstructed a public officer
In the discharge or attempted discharge of their duty
notes: Broader than resisting arrest — covers obstructing any official function. Providing false identification to an officer also prosecuted under § 148.9.

elements: Defendant engaged in conduct described in one of the subsections of § 647
Including public intoxication, solicitation, peeping, or lodging in public places without consent
notes: California's disorderly conduct covers multiple types of behavior including public intoxication (§ 647(f)), solicitation (§ 647(b)), and peeping/invasion of privacy (§ 647(j)).

elements: Defendant was found in a public place
While under the influence of intoxicating liquor, drugs, controlled substance, toluene, or any combination thereof
Defendant was unable to exercise care for their own safety or the safety of others, OR was interfering with or obstructing the free use of a street, sidewalk, or other public way
notes: Many jurisdictions offer civil protective custody (72-hour hold) instead of criminal prosecution. Third or subsequent offense within 12 months may be referred to treatment.

elements: Defendant unlawfully fought in a public place, OR challenged another person to fight in a public place, OR maliciously and willfully disturbed another person by loud and unreasonable noise, OR used offensive words in a public place likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction
notes: Often offered as a plea bargain reduction for more serious charges (assault, battery, DUI). Can be filed as an infraction with a fine only, or as a misdemeanor.

elements: Defendant willfully entered or remained on property belonging to another
Without permission or right
After being asked to leave or in violation of posted signs
enhancements: Aggravated trespassing with credible threat (Cal. Penal Code § 601 — wobbler, up to 3 years)
notes: Multiple forms of trespass under § 602. First offense trespass on posted land is typically an infraction. Aggravated trespass (§ 601) involves entering property within 30 days of making a credible threat.

penalty_max: 5 years (felony: 16mo-2-3 triad, enhanced with priors); 1 year (misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant willfully, maliciously, and repeatedly followed or harassed another person
Defendant made a credible threat with the intent to place that person in reasonable fear for their safety or the safety of their immediate family
enhancements: Violation of restraining order (felony mandatory under § 646.9(b))
notes: Cyberstalking included. Restraining order violations elevate to mandatory felony. Can be prosecuted alongside domestic violence charges.

statute_title: Harassment by Telephone or Electronic Communication
elements: Defendant used a telephone or electronic communication device
To make repeated contact with another person
With intent to annoy, harass, or threaten
Using obscene language, threats, or repeated calls
notes: Covers phone calls, text messages, emails, and social media. Civil harassment restraining orders available under Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 527.6.

elements: A valid protective order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant willfully violated the order
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours (second violation within 1 year involving violence under § 273.6(d))
enhancements: Prior conviction for violating a protective order (wobbler)
notes: Applies to domestic violence protective orders, civil harassment restraining orders, elder abuse orders, and gun violence restraining orders. Second violation within a year with violence is a wobbler.

elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a court order
Or engaged in disorderly, contemptuous, or insolent behavior toward the judge
notes: Includes violations of court orders not covered by specific protective order statutes. Both criminal and civil contempt available.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle upon a highway or in an off-street parking facility
In willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property
enhancements: Causing injury (6 months, up to $1,000 fine under § 23104)
Speed contest (§ 23109 — up to 90 days, $1,000 fine)
notes: Often used as plea bargain reduction from DUI (wet reckless under § 23103.5). Wet reckless counts as prior DUI for enhancement purposes within 10 years.

statute_title: Driving on a Suspended or Revoked License
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle
While their driving privilege was suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
enhancements: DUI-related suspension (Cal. Veh. Code § 14601.2 — 10 days mandatory, up to 1 year)
Habitual traffic offender (Cal. Veh. Code § 14601.3 — 30 days mandatory)
notes: Knowledge element can be proven by DMV mailing of notice. Multiple code sections apply depending on reason for suspension: § 14601.1 (general), § 14601.2 (DUI), § 14601.5 (BAC refusal).

penalty_max: 6 months (property); 4 years (felony injury: 16mo-2-3 triad or 2-3-4 triad with permanent injury)
elements: Defendant was involved in a vehicle accident
Defendant knew they were involved in the accident
Defendant failed to stop and provide required information and/or render aid
mandatory_minimum: 90 days (felony hit-and-run causing death or permanent serious injury under § 20001(b)(2))
enhancements: Death or permanent serious injury (wobbler under § 20001(b)(2))
notes: Property damage hit-and-run is always a misdemeanor. Injury/death hit-and-run is a wobbler. Must stop, identify yourself, and render reasonable assistance.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (§ 2800.1); Wobbler (§ 2800.2 reckless); Felony (§ 2800.3 causing injury/death)
penalty_max: 1 year (misdemeanor); 3 years (felony reckless: 16mo-2-3 triad); 7 years (causing death/GBI under § 2800.3)
elements: Defendant fled or attempted to evade a pursuing peace officer's vehicle
The officer's vehicle was distinctively marked and had red light, siren, and was operated by an officer in uniform
Defendant willfully fled with intent to evade
enhancements: Causing death or serious bodily injury (felony under § 2800.3)
notes: Misdemeanor evasion requires only willful flight. Felony evasion requires reckless driving during pursuit. Causing injury or death during evasion is a separate felony.

statute_title: Open Container in a Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant was a driver or passenger in a motor vehicle on a highway
Defendant possessed an open alcoholic beverage container
notes: Infraction only — no jail time. Driver and passenger versions. Open marijuana container in vehicle covered under Cal. Veh. Code § 23222(b).

statute_title: Refusal of Chemical Test (Implied Consent Violation)
penalty_max: Additional 48 hours jail (first DUI); additional 96 hours (second DUI); additional 10 days (third DUI)
elements: Defendant was lawfully arrested for DUI
Defendant was informed of the consequences of refusal
Defendant refused to submit to or complete a chemical test
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours additional (first DUI with refusal); 96 hours (second); 10 days (third)
notes: Not a standalone charge but enhances DUI penalties. Also triggers automatic 1-year administrative license suspension (first offense) by DMV. Preliminary Alcohol Screening (PAS) test is optional for non-probationers over 21.

offense_class: Varies (up to maximum sentence for original offense)
penalty_max: Maximum sentence for the original offense
elements: Defendant was granted probation on a criminal case
Defendant violated a term or condition of that probation
notes: Court can revoke, modify, or reinstate probation. Standard of proof is preponderance of evidence, not beyond a reasonable doubt. No right to jury trial. Court can impose any sentence originally available.

elements: Defendant was on probation
Defendant violated a technical condition (missed appointment, failed drug test, travel violation, etc.)
notes: Technical violations include missed check-ins, failed drug tests, curfew violations, travel without permission. Courts increasingly use graduated sanctions for technical violations rather than revocation.

statute_title: Substantive Violation of Probation (New Criminal Conduct)
penalty_max: Maximum sentence for original offense plus sentence for new offense
elements: Defendant was on probation
Defendant committed a new criminal offense while on probation
notes: New criminal conduct while on probation is a substantive violation. Can result in revocation and imposition of the full sentence for the original offense, plus charges for the new offense.

penalty_max: 180 days (revocation term); return to prison for new felony
elements: Defendant was on parole from state prison
Defendant violated a condition of parole
notes: Under Realignment (AB 109), most parole violations are handled by local courts with county jail flash incarceration (up to 10 days) or revocation terms (up to 180 days). Serious or violent offenders may be returned to state prison.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (released on own recognizance); Felony (released on bail in felony case under § 1320.5)
elements: Defendant was released from custody on own recognizance or bail
Defendant willfully failed to appear as required by the court
Defendant had the intent to evade the process of the court
notes: Bench warrant issued upon failure to appear. Felony FTA (§ 1320.5) requires proof of intent to evade court process. Bail may be forfeited.

elements: Defendant reported to a peace officer that a felony or misdemeanor had been committed
Defendant knew the report was false
notes: Covers false reports of crimes and false reports to 911. Separate statute for false fire alarm (§ 148.4). Making a false report of an emergency under § 148.3 is a wobbler.

elements: Defendant solicited another person to engage in an act of prostitution
Defendant intended to engage in that act
Defendant did something beyond merely asking — took a step in furtherance
enhancements: Solicitation of a minor (felony under Cal. Penal Code § 647(b)(4))
notes: SB 357 (2022) decriminalized loitering for prostitution. The act of solicitation remains criminal. Second offense requires minimum 45 days. Soliciting a minor is a felony.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first); Wobbler (second or in inhabited dwelling)
elements: Defendant willfully exposed their private parts in a public place or in a place where others were present who would be offended
Defendant acted with the intent to direct public attention to their genitals for the purpose of sexually gratifying themselves or another, or sexually offending another
notes: Requires specific intent for sexual purposes. First offense is misdemeanor with sex offender registration. Second offense or aggravated indecent exposure is a wobbler.

elements: Defendant loitered, prowled, or wandered upon the private property of another
At any time, without visible or lawful business with the owner or occupant
notes: Must be on private property. SB 357 repealed loitering for prostitution. Some local loitering ordinances have been struck down as unconstitutionally vague.

offense_class: Wobbler (same punishment as the target offense)
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more other persons to commit a crime
At least one member of the conspiracy performed an overt act in furtherance of the agreement
The overt act was performed in California
notes: Punished the same as the target offense (or the most serious target offense if multiple). Conspiracy to commit a felony is a felony. Conspiracy to commit a misdemeanor is a wobbler. Each conspirator is liable for all reasonably foreseeable crimes committed by co-conspirators.

penalty_max: 4 years (for transactions exceeding $150,000 in 30 days) or 3 years (for $5,000-$150,000)
elements: Defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
Through a financial institution
With the specific intent to promote, manage, establish, carry on, or facilitate criminal activity
Transaction value exceeded $5,000 in a 7-day period or $25,000 in a 30-day period
notes: Separate from federal money laundering statutes. California-specific thresholds and penalties. Often charged alongside drug trafficking and organized crime offenses.

elements: Defendant willfully caused or permitted unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering to an elder (65+) or dependent adult
OR defendant willfully caused or permitted the elder/dependent adult to be placed in a situation likely to endanger health
enhancements: Great bodily injury (additional 5 years if victim is 70+ under § 368(b)(2))
notes: Covers physical abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, and emotional abuse. Enhanced penalties for financial exploitation based on amount: additional 1 year (>$950), 2 years (>$65,000), 3 years (>$200,000), 4 years (>$1.3M).

elements: Defendant intentionally distributed an image of the intimate body part or parts of another identifiable person
The image was obtained or created under circumstances where there was an agreement that it would not be distributed
Distribution caused serious emotional distress
Defendant knew or should have known distribution would cause distress
notes: California's 'revenge porn' law. Civil remedies also available under Cal. Civ. Code § 1708.85. Distribution of images of a minor is prosecuted under child exploitation statutes.

statute_title: Failure to Register as a Sex Offender
offense_class: Wobbler (Felony or Misdemeanor depending on underlying offense)
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender under Cal. Penal Code § 290
Defendant willfully failed to register or update registration as required
enhancements: Underlying offense was a violent or serious felony (felony mandatory)
notes: Must register within 5 working days of moving. Annual re-registration required within 5 working days of birthday. Under SB 384 (2021), tiered registration: Tier 1 (10 years), Tier 2 (20 years), Tier 3 (lifetime).

elements: Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain a controlled substance
By fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, subterfuge, or concealment of a material fact
Including using a false name, giving a false address, or falsely representing to a doctor that they are not receiving a controlled substance from another doctor
notes: Commonly called 'doctor shopping.' The CURES database (Controlled Substance Utilization Review and Evaluation System) helps detect prescription fraud. Physicians also face liability.

statute_title: Wire Fraud (Federal — Commonly Charged in California)
penalty_max: 20 years (30 years if affecting a financial institution)
elements: Defendant devised or participated in a scheme to defraud
Defendant acted with intent to defraud
Defendant used or caused the use of interstate wire communications in furtherance of the scheme
enhancements: Affecting a financial institution (30 years, $1M fine)
Involving a presidentially declared disaster or emergency
notes: Federal charge — prosecuted in U.S. District Court. Any use of phone, internet, email, or electronic transfer satisfies the wire communication element. Frequently paired with mail fraud and conspiracy charges.

penalty_max: 5 years (state); 20 years (if charged federally under 15 U.S.C. § 78ff)
elements: Defendant willfully made an untrue statement of a material fact or omitted a material fact
In connection with the offer, sale, or purchase of a security
With intent to deceive or defraud investors
notes: Can be prosecuted under state (California Corporate Securities Law) or federal (Securities Exchange Act) law. SEC civil enforcement is separate from criminal prosecution.

elements: Defendant had sexual intercourse with another person
The other person did not consent
Accomplished by force, violence, duress, menace, or fear of bodily injury, OR victim incapable of consent
enhancements: One Strike law (§ 667.61 — 15 or 25 years to life)
notes: Strike offense. Mandatory sex offender registration. One Strike law applies with specified aggravating factors (kidnapping, use of weapon, prior sex offense). Spousal rape prosecuted under § 262.

statute_title: Castle Doctrine — Presumption of Fear in Home
elements: Defendant was inside their own residence
Another person unlawfully and forcibly entered or was entering the residence
Defendant knew or had reason to believe an unlawful, forcible entry occurred
Defendant used force, including deadly force, against the intruder
notes: California follows a modified Castle Doctrine — presumption of reasonable fear when a person forcibly enters your home. No duty to retreat inside your home. Outside the home, self-defense requires reasonable belief of imminent danger and proportional force (Cal. Penal Code § 197-199).

elements: Defendant was on post-release community supervision
Defendant violated a condition of supervision
notes: Under Realignment (AB 109), many offenders released to PRCS instead of state parole. Revocation handled by superior court, not Board of Parole Hearings. Maximum revocation term is 180 days.

elements: Elements vary by specific offense
notes: Catch-all category for California criminal offenses not specifically categorized. Includes Cal. Penal Code, Health & Safety Code, Vehicle Code, Business & Professions Code, and other California statutory offenses.
